questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhomogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t)-4 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t)+y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $0$ |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{5(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{5t}-\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by integrating both sides from $0$ to 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ at $t=0$ gives

$$
y(0)={e}^{-A\cdot 0}x(0)=Ix(0)=x(0).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t=0.$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$
